chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār said:

I asked Abā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) about a man who has one hundred dirhams and ten dinars: is there zakāt upon him? He said, 'If he fled from zakāt with it, then zakāt is upon him.' I said, 'He did not flee with it; he inherited one hundred dirhams and ten dinars.' He said, 'There is no zakāt upon him.' I said, 'So he should not break the dirhams into dinars, nor the dinars into dirhams?' He said, 'No.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And there is no harm in paying the gold from the silver by value, and paying the silver from the gold by value, and paying the barley from the wheat by its value, and paying the wheat from the barley by its value. -(271)
That is indicated by what was narrated - Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad from al-Barqī from Abū Jaʿfar al-Thānī (peace be upon him)

He said: I wrote to him, 'May I be your ransom, is it permissible that what is obligatory from the crops be paid from wheat and barley, and what is obligatory on gold be paid as dirhams by the value of what it is worth, or is it not permissible except that from each thing what is in it be paid?' So he answered him (peace be upon him), 'Whichever is easier, that is to be paid.'
ai.seo_question: Can I pay zakat on gold using silver or cash value instead of the gold itself?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that inherited wealth is not immediately subject to zakāt unless the owner intentionally delays payment to avoid the obligation, establishing a principle of leniency for new wealth holders. It further permits paying zakāt on one type of asset (e.g., gold) using the monetary value of another (e.g., silver dirhams), reflecting the Shia juristic view that zakāt is a monetary obligation rather than strictly in-kind. This flexibility allows for practical ease in distribution while maintaining the economic value of the due portion.
